subsubtopic: SPILL OF PCB CHEMICAL AT REGINA, SASK.-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, which I trust will meet with the approval of the House.
In view of the alarming spill at the city of Regina of a least 1,500 gallons of Askral, a PCB, a chemical that has been linked to cancer, birth defects and other ailments, this being the biggest known spill of PCBs in Canadian history, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro):
That the House instruct the minister of the environment to make provision in his department and in co-operation with provincial environment departments for the establishment of a detection and correction squad, being an investigative and action-oriented task force which in the future could act quickly on such industrial spills as have occurred in Regina and at Dowling, near Sudbury, thus affording protection to the health and safety of Canadians and literally saving millions of taxpayers' dollars.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce today that, based on conclusions of one of the most thorough evaluations of a defence procurement program ever carried out in this country, cabinet has now approved a set of directions regarding the next
November 23, 1978

stage of the process towards acquisition of a new fighter aircraft for the Canadian Forces.
In arriving at these conclusions I have been guided by, and the judgments reflect, the military advice which I have received from the Chief of the Defence Staff. The government, through the offices of the NFA program manager, has now informed four of the competing manufacturers that their aircraft are no longer in the competition. These are: Grumman with the F-14 Tomcat; McDonnell-Douglas with the F-15 Eagle; Panavia with the Tornado, and Northrop with the CF-18L Cobra.
The finalists will be the General Dynamics CF-16 and the McDonnell-Douglas/Northrop CF-18A, which are the Canadian versions of these aircraft. The government has also decided against further consideration of a mixed fleet of fighters. The governments of the Federal Republic of Germany, Great Britain, Italy and United States, which all have been following this selection process with keen interest, are also being informed of this development.
Direction has now been given to the interdepartmental program office to initiate discussions leading to the negotiation of draft contracts with the two prime manufacturers remaining in competition. In addition to the very important questions of aircraft capability, fleet size, delivery schedule, and optimum phasing of payments, emphasis will be placed on negotiating the best mix of industrial benefits for Canada. In these negotiations particular attention will be paid to arrangements that could contribute to the growth of research and development activity in Canada, as well as high technology industry which complements our geography and resources. Emphasis also will be given to ensuring that all regions of the country will have full opportunity to participate in this program.
I expect that it will be several months before I am in a position to present a comparative analysis of draft contracts to cabinet for final selection of a new fighter aircraft. I am sure that those of you who have followed the evolution of the program since its start, in March, 1977, have come to realize the magnitude of the task facing the government in this selection process. At the end of June, as you will recall, the government decided to allow additional time to permit manufacturers to refine their initial proposals. I am pleased to report that by the new deadline of August 1 all had responded with offers that contained substantial improvements over their earlier proposals.
Our numerical requirement of between 130 and 150 aircraft is critical to our capability to meet our domestic and European commitments. We are indeed disappointed that procurement of sufficient numbers of F-14s, F-15s or Tornados could not be accommodated within our set budget of $2.34 billion in August 1977 dollars.
Our evaluation also revealed that acquisition of a mixed fleet would bring little or no benefit in terms of fleet size and that operation of such a fleet would bring substantial liabili-
National Defence
ties, including double training and logistics support systems over the life span of the aircraft.
The two most severe constraints that we face, and will continue to face, are the number of aircraft required and the set amount of money to buy them. Our task, then, is to buy the best military aircraft available within those constraints, while seeking the best possible industrial benefits with a minimum of project risk.
In addition to cost and numbers, there are other considerations that serve to favour the two aircraft we have kept in the process. To begin with, there is the military and political assessment that we have made of the current-and to a certain extent, anticipated-strategic situation that we are facing.
We have come to the conclusion that an adequate number of the smaller aircraft equipped with radar guided air-to-air missiles and suitably deployed across Canada, could afford us the capability to exercise our sovereignty fully by intercepting, identifying, and if necessary, destroying aircraft that might be probing into Canadian airspace. Having this type of prudent capability, we believe, would deter probes and offer adequate protection against the possibility of a bomber attack on the North American continent.
Having eliminated the three most expensive systems from the competition, three remained-the CF-16, the CF-18A and the CF-18L-that met or came very close to meeting our numerical requirements within the budgetary envelope while being able to meet the most likely military challenges.
The CF-18L proposed by Northrop could meet these most likely challenges and probably be acquired in sufficient quantities. Potentially, it also provides a very attractive package of industrial benefits. However, we have assessed as very considerable the risk of committing Canada to buying a sophisticated aircraft that is not in service with any other country. At this time, I consider all the various types of risks which could be involved in the development and initial introduction into operational service of this aircraft are greater than we either need or are prepared to accept. Moreover, even in the best of circumstances, the delivery schedule of the CF-18L is likely to be markedly behind that required for the timely replacement of our CF-101 and CF-104 aircraft.
The CF-16 is a single-engine aircraft which has been selected by five of our NATO allies, including the United States. Should the CF-16 be acquired, Canada would of course have extensive commonality with NATO allies in Europe. While this aircraft does not have the degree of sophistication of the larger aircraft, it does have acceptable capability and is the only aircraft which at this point meets the numbers required.
The other fighter remaining in the competition, the CF-18A, offers us another set of possibilities. It may be more expensive than the CF-16 would be; therefore we can expect to acquire fewer, although I am optimistic that an adequate number to meet our roles can be acquired in negotiations. Purchase of this aircraft could allow for co-operative logistics arrangements with the United States.

November 23, 1978
National Defence
On the other hand, being a twin-engined, somewhat larger aircraft, the CF-18A offers some definite advantages of its own. These include a good potential for growth, or a capability to be fitted with new systems that may be necessary to cater to future demands made of a fighter aircraft. The CF-18A also currently has more advanced all-weather capabilities in the context of sovereignty protection and air defence.
We must recognize, however, that in both military and political terms, a major consideration for Canada is collective security in Europe. This is where the philosophy, or strategy, of deterrence, common to all members of the NATO alliance, is subject to its greatest challenge, in the light of qualitative and quantitative improvements to the forces of the Warsaw Pact countries.
It is important that our own contributions to collective security be quantitatively and qualitatively adequate for deterrence. Quantitatively, this means a number of aircraft at least equal to that we now commit to the Alliance in central Europe and to the northern flank. This total number of aircraft, plus some for training and attrition, makes up well over half of our total requirement. This is clearly a factor that influences the type of capability that we must seek in the fleet, the qualitative aspect of the contribution. We want that capability to be prudently adequate for the sovereignty and air defence roles in Canada and also to be effective in particular roles in central Europe and in northern Norway.
As you can appreciate, there are pros and cons to both types of aircraft. I can assure you that there were also some pros and cons to all aircraft that have now been eliminated. Our request for proposal provided a standard which enabled us to obtain truly comparable data for all contenders. No single aircraft could possibly have met all specifications given in the request for proposal. Nor was it the government's intention to acquire an aircraft whose capabilities far exceeded those required to carry out assessed roles adequately.
We are convinced that we have now made a very judicious decision in selecting these two aircraft for further consideration, taking into account the factors of military requirements, budgetary considerations, the minimum number of aircraft required, the risk element, and the potential industrial benefits.
We expect that a reduction to two contenders will have a very favourable impact on Canadian industry's ability to participate with prime manufacturers in the development of detailed industrial proposals.
To the prime manufacturers who have devoted considerable resources to this competition so far, and particularly to manufacturers' representatives who have displayed so much energy and sincere efforts in presenting their companies' proposals in the best possible light, we owe thanks for their exceptional co-operation.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I am confident that in this next, critical phase of the fighter program, the interdepartmental team and all others who are in any way involved will continue

to work in an atmosphere of fair and keen competition, and that rapid progress will be made towards selection of a new fighter aircraft to meet Canada's needs to the end of the century.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our party has for many years advocated that movement should be made by the government to re-equip our forces. Normally I would be very pleased at the announcement-the announcement of any progress brings with it a certain amount of gratification, I suppose. However, to say the least, the statement the minister has made today is very unusual. In the very short time available to me since I received the statement only a few minutes ago, I have made some notes. I would have preferred to have had more time, but if I cut my remarks fairly short now, perhaps I will be able to make it up by the number of questions I am allowed to put. I see at least ten outstanding questions which have not been dealt with in the minister's statement and which have a considerable bearing on the new fighter aircraft.
First, I would point out that the minister states they have been guided-I presume he is referring to the cabinet-and adds:
The judgments reflect the military advice which I have received from the Chief of the Defence Staff.
That is a rather peculiar admission when one understands that most of the consideration was done by a project team. I am already beginning to hear disturbing rumours that the project team's advice was largely ignored in the selection and that the cabinet called together another group of senior civil servants at the deputy minister level to rewrite the proposal which was given to the Chief of Defence Staff and to the minister in early September. That is one of the reasons for the unseemly delay we have undergone so far.
Elsewhere in his statement the minister said:
Emphasis will be given to ensuring that all regions of the country will have full opportunity to participate in this program.
That bears a striking resemblance to the long range patrol aircraft proposition which was put to us, under which all parts of the country were to have an opportunity to participate in the offset work and the industrial benefits. As I pointed out to the House the other day, British Columbia so far has managed to obtain one half of one per cent. To a province that has 10 per cent of the population and an industrial capacity to match, this hardly indicates that anyone out west has reason to dance in the streets over the work they are going to get out of any project this government offers. Their reputation is too well known at present.
Again, the minister said:
Our evaluation reveals that acquisition of a mixed fleet would bring little or no benefit and would bring substantial liabilities, including double training in logistic support systems over the life span of the aircraft.
This, of course, does not stop them from flying three different types of fighter at the present time. It never seems to stop Air Canada from buying different planes from different companies. In my opinion, the statement is merely included to
November 23, 1978

validate a bad decision rather than as containing any truth insofar as problems from having two or three different types of fighter plane are concerned. I have yet to hear the minister or anyone else in a senior position in defence complaining bitterly that we have F-104s in Europe and F-lOls in Canada.
On page four of his statement the minister says he came to the conclusion that an adequate number of smaller aircraft equipped with radar guided air to air missiles could afford us the capability to exercise our sovereignty fully. No mention was made of the range of the two fighter aircraft which the announcement tells us have been selected. I would have been more pleased if the minister had managed to discover the range of the F-16 and the F-18 as compared, say, to the F-15.
Later we find the minister saying that the F-16 has acceptable capability and is the only aircraft which to this point meets the numbers required. Then in another part of his statement he said that unfortunately the F-18L, I believe it was, could not quite make it in terms of the numbers they would be able to provide, and that the F-15 could not make it for the same reason within the limitations of $2.34 billion. Now if the F-16 is the only one, it means that its running mate, the F-18L, also cannot qualify under the same set of regulations that caused the minister to turn down the F-15, the F-14, and the larger and more expensive planes. Either they had a dividing line there or they did not. It is my understanding they could have provided about 117 F-15 planes within the $2.34 billion limit, and there is certainly no doubt in anyone's mind that the F-15 was far closer to being the favourite of the project team than the F-16 or the F-18 A.
The final choice, as the minister said, comes down to the F-18A and the F-16, and I must question whether the 18A is in there just as a straw man to be used by the government to get betters bids out of General Dynamics, because the F-18, let's face it Mr. Speaker, belongs on an aircraft carrier. It carries around some 2,500 pounds of surplus machinery which enables it to land and take off from carriers, and unless the minister intends to buy a carrier, or buy back a carrier, 1 see no reason why we would want to select the F-18A over, say, the F-18L. I realize there is a difference in the time at which they would be available and I hope to bring this out in my questioning. However, it seems to me a most peculiar choice of planes has been made by the minister, considering the preferences expressed by his project team. I hope I will be given the opportunity to carry out lengthy questioning later on today as to the reasons for the unusual choice.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, think it necessary to comment on the fact that on a matter involving well over $2 billion we received notice of this statement only a few minutes before it was delivered in the House. I must in all fairness add, though, that it does not embarrass me one little bit because the point of view we take makes the total exercise of choosing between different suppliers irrelevant.
We think that what the government should be doing is looking at the total strategic purpose which lies behind this proposition to acquire between 130 and 150 fighter planes. It
National Defence
is our view that this is a misapplication of roles, that it is going back to something which is totally obsolete, something which has nothing to do with the security of Canada or the stability of the world as a whole.
So far as I know, we have never had a clear statement of the strategic purpose of what is the largest purchase of military equipment ever made by Canada-the minister can correct me if I am wrong. We have never been told the nature of the threat which is to be met. We know that the fighter planes based in North America are intended to replace a number of Voodoos and other aircraft which were designed to meet the threat of a manned bomber attack. Indeed, the statement just made by the minister does contain a reference to the possible threat of the manned bomber. We do not believe in the reality of that threat.
We think that the role of a government or of anyone making decisions in this field, should be to look at the basic situation and then fit the equipment into the roles which are necessary. We say that a manned bomber threat is unthinkable at the present stage of history, the missile age. Aeroplanes involved in attacking Canada and the United States would have to travel two or three hours. Their coming presumably would be made well known to the American defence system, by the forms of detection which are in existence. We believe in the necessity of such detection, and if it is not adequate, let us improve it.
However, once we have adequate detection, the defence which exists both for Canada and the United States as far as North America is concerned, is the fact that the Americans have available defences in submarines and elsewhere to meet any first strike. Perhaps, fixed missile sites are no longer as secure as they used to be for the placing of the strategic weapons of the United States, but as far as submarines are concerned, the whole society of the U.S.S.R., could be blanked out.
With adequate mechanisms the targets of attack would not be there. It seems we have to assume an irrationality on the part of the leaders of the U.S.S.R. which, whatever else some of us may say or think about them, is totally inconsistent with the facts.
We say we should not be choosing between this and that. This proposition will cost $2.3 billion in 1977 dollars. We must add to that the extra cost of inflation and any other extra costs which may be involved by reason of our present exchange rate. I think somewhere around $3 billion would be a modest figure to expect. What could be done with $3 billion? Many things need to be done. I propose to speak in the budget debate on this very subject and to elaborate on the points I am making now.
I know that this is an occasion for brief statements, but we say to the government that it ought to look at this all over again. We need a clear strategic statement. From time to time the minister has made highly exuberant and optimistic assertions, but he confines himself to assertions like "It is necessary for the security of Canada." Let him show us why he says it is

November 23, 1978
National Defence
necessary. What threats have to be met, and how real are they? Is this just a fantasy against which we are supposed to defend ourselves? We think it is, and therefore to be picking one fighter plane against another is not necessary.
I want to say a word about offsets. I will have more to say on this subject when I participate in the budget debate. It is, of course, a good idea to have offsets, including our technology, but at the present time the aircraft industry is very buoyant, and what we need is improvement in the technology for the things we can sell commercially. We do not need to build up our capacity to supply sophisticated weaponry to the countries of the world. Perhaps they would buy it. The insanity which pervades this world is such that $400 billion per year is spent on armaments, which have no purpose but destruction, even at a time when human needs throughout the world cry out for attention, capital, and personnel.
All we can say regarding this statement is that it is not too late to look at the reality of this situation. The commitment has not been finalized. Let the government look at the reality of this situation and then tell us, if it is possible, where, why, and how it proposes to undertake this colossal expenditure. Why is it necessary for the security of Canada or the stability of the world? I wish the minister were coming before us and saying that we are moving into the field of so-called smart bombs, which are precision guided weapons which hold out a much greater hope to small countries. These are light weapons, armed with laser guides, which can hit targets. They are highly effective in stopping tanks and in shooting down fighter planes.
We know we have obligations. When I have a chance to speak in the budget debate I will set forth the important obligations Canada can meet in the military sphere. We must meet them. That naturally will cost money, and the job must be done well. There is no point in doing a thing half-heartedly, but for goodness sake let us not be led astray by this mirage of an attack, which no sane person would ever make upon North America in this missile age. Granted, conditions can change, but I am talking about conditions as they exist now.
The government should look at the whole thing again, and consider it from beginning to end. It is not just a matter of which is better and which is worse. I am sure that if the government considers the whole matter again it will arrive at a decision which will be far more beneficial to the people of Canada in this time of strain and so-called restraint and retrenchment. A re-examination of this matter would be far more important than any other contribution the government has made in the past few years.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make very brief comments on the statement the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) just delivered to the House. I want to thank the minister for making available to me a copy of his statement which I received only around three o'clock. I do not feel strongly about that because at 1.30 I received a phone call, probably from his office, telling me that I was

about to get a copy of his speech. But given the fact that the postal service is very poor, the minister is obviously not responsible for the delay. Hon. members who spoke about the minister's statement before me said the same thing.
But I do not have only bad things to say. I want to seize the first occasion I have to thank the minister from the bottom of my heart for having authorized the band of the Royal 22nd Regiment to come to Montmagny on Remembrance Day. On such a beautiful day the local residents were very happy to see a detachment of the armed forces and the air cadets and I can assure him that that is a good way to ensure harmony exists in our country. You should have seen the onlookers! For the first in the 12 years I have witnessed such ceremonies I saw people give rousing cheers. It is a sign of the times and I am very happy that the minister authorized such a visit to our city of Montmagny.
Mr. Speaker, at the time of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) visit to Bonn for the summit conference, I also remember seeing on TV our Prime Minister surrounded by aircraft manufacturers trying to convince him that their type of aircraft was the best. Canada was really the centre of attention. We could see that for those manufacturers this was a big occasion to make a deal. Some businessmen from different countries were also present.
The Minister of Defence has just announced that we need to buy between 130 and 150 fighter planes. I assume, or at least I hope that these will not be used in a new world war but that they will help those who really want to maintain peace in the world. Canada is prepared to do its share, but to do so, it must be well equipped. I had a few occasions to visit countries throughout the world where our armed forces do an examplary job, a tremendous job to preserve peace. Naturally, there is the odd trouble here and there, little conflicts that break out, but were it not for the NATO force in which Canada participates, unfortunately I think we would have faced major military confrontations. I believe it most deeply. However, I must say that I am not an aircraft specialist. I trust the experts in that field whose duty is to advise the minister. I hope their advice is in the best interest of Canada rather than in the best interest of those who want to make money at our expenses.
I fully understand that it is normal to make profits even in manufacturing aircraft, but we should also make sure that our money is not wasted. I am sure the minister is smart enough to detect those who might try to profit from the circumstances to take advantage of him and convince him that some type of aircraft is better than some other type, without he being sure that it is the truth. Thus, the minister tells us that he chose the CF-16 rather than the CF-18A. I hope he is not mistaken.
But I would like to ask something of the minister. We are being told that the contracts have not been signed, that the details are still under study. I would like to suggest-the minister made reference to that point in his statement-that we go further than that. All kinds of parts will be needed to
November 23, 1978

build those planes, to put them together. Obviously those parts, like in the automobile industry, can be manufactured in Quebec city, in Trois-Rivieres, in Sherbrooke or even in Mont-magny where the unemployment rate reaches 30 per cent. These parts could then be sent to companies for assembly. It should then be seen that the Canadian industrial sector benefit from these contracts, that it be given the opportunity to manufacture some of these parts. This would enable us to create jobs in this country and to make a good deal with other countries.
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the minister has a rather sizable budget and that he must do his utmost to apply the principles of moderation while providing our armed forces with the equipment required. This is essential. So I would like the minister to inform us more regularly of what happens in his department as concerns not only the organization of the air force but also the equipment needs of our armed forces, our naval forces and our vessels.
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to remind the minister that two or three times he announced shipbuilding projects to meet the needs of our armed forces for national defence. I would ask him whether it would be possible to accelerate this decision to help our shipyards keep up with the times, keep up with their more sophisticated competitors and give them the opportunity to provide jobs for the many unemployed Canadians. So, if we are to make a decision as it is required, we should make it when unemployment is at its highest level.
I think it is more important to spend money in a way which encourages the use of our manpower and our expertise rather than to pay those people to do nothing and make them loose the desire to work, because after a while you finally believe it is not necessary to work and you find it difficult to go back on the labour market.
Mr. Speaker, I have here a document I have just received, the Right to Information. Parliament, ministers and courts. Who said this? The government. Here again, I wish we were better informed. In parliament particularly we can understand when we are informed of the facts. And if we have suggestions to make, we are responsible enough, I think, to do it and instead of being prejudicial to the minister it would help him exercise his difficult responsibilities as Minister of National Defence.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I shall try to keep my questions as short as I can, and I hope that the answers will be equally brief because I have several questions that I wish to get through. subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure that it is in the best interest of the program to produce at this time the industrial benefits or their regional location. November 23, 1978
National Defence
I think the hon. member may be assured that the greatest effort will be made in this regard. subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Could the minister tell the House how many planes in each case is the short list of tenders offering? How many planes of each type are there?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Based on the best assessment, the CF-18A comes close enough to the 130 minimum that we required, with a reasonable expectation of exceeding that when we get to the final negotiations. Mr. Speaker, I am rather disappointed about the last answer; I would rather do without the adjectives and adverbs and find out how many planes are involved, which was the question I asked, whether the number be 137, 127 or 117. I understand that for the CF-15 they were able to bid 117 planes.

My understanding is it was turned down because the Mirage 2000 was not yet in flight, but it would appear that the F-18L lasted until today. It seems that the French company was cut off rather summarily back in January of last year, yet the F-18L, which the minister says will not be ready in time, which is one of the reasons he turned it down, was considered right up until now.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: The Mirage 2000 team themselves withdrew, Mr. Speaker. It was not our assessment; they themselves said that they did not believe they would be ready in adequate time and they did not believe they could marshal a sufficiently attractive industrial benefit package, and on their own volition they withdrew from the competition, really before it started.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the minister, first of all, to inform the House what is the present assignment of fighter planes as between North America and our European theatre. My understanding is that we have an air group of 45 planes in Europe, and the minister's statement seemed to lead toward the view that we are now going to equalize somehow or other our commitment, which would seem, if my figures are right, to mean a substantial increase in our commitment to NATO, one that is far beyond our commitment of ground forces there or anything relative to that, with a diminution in our commitment to North America. Perhaps he could say, in this new dispensation-I am sure they are not all allocated yet because they are not even built or ordered yet-what is the proposed distribution of the 130 to 150 planes as between the two different theatres, the North American and the European theatres?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the number is precisely the same as now, namely, 36 assigned and, I believe, 18 in reserve, for the central front, and 24 aircraft for the north flank. That commitment will remain the same. At the present time there is a larger total fleet. There was a figure I ran across of 160 total front line, but with these new aircraft of all models there will be a much, much lower attribution because of the higher technology and safety features put into them. Because it is only one type of aircraft there will be a reduction in the number we need in our training and replacement systems. So there is a one for one replacement there.
I think that what might have led the hon. member to that conclusion is the ability to maintain our sovereignty role, which I would take from the hon. member's remarks today and at other times he still considers rather important. Protection without enforcement does not leave us with sovereignty; it just leaves us with information. We need something to enforce that sovereignty, and that role we will fulfil with the same number of aircraft, I believe 36 being assigned to that specific role.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have only one question to ask since the minister has just replied to many of the questions I was asking myself and since my colleagues have asked very specific questions. I would like to know the approximate cost of the CF-16 and CF-18A aircraft and whether that cost includes all the equipment needed to enable those planes to fulfil their role.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I have not broken this down in fly away cost per aircraft, though I am sure I can get that; but the $2.34 billion program covers equipment, manuals, spare parts and training systems, implemented with enough reserves in each case to provide adequately for our needs.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Since the minister has quoted the figure of $2.3 billion and since the figures we have been given for the number of planes vary from 130 to 150, there is

November 23, 1978

quite a difference. Could we at least have an approximate figure? Will we go over $2.3 billion to purchase 130, 140 or 150 aircraft? This is where the unit price can make a difference. Could we know the approximate cost of these aircraft?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are attempting within that budget of $2.34 billion to acquire 150 aircraft. That will allow us to do our job, to fulfil our roles on a one to one basis for our training system, and give us sufficient back-up aircraft to account for natural attrition. As for the price, if one takes a very much ball park figure-I am sure that people who sell aircraft would not do it in this way-I always talk about a $10 million aircraft and a $20 million aircraft. If we look at it in terms of a $10 million aircraft for individual fly away cost, then that would be reasonable. One of the studies that I have read, and I have read many in connection with this program, indicated it would be about $1 'A billion for the aircraft program itself. The rest goes towards support for the particular items about which the hon. member is concerned. Those are not the precise figures, but I would be pleased to get them for him.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have two questions, unless some of the replies lead to further ones. First, now that it has been determined there is to be one aircraft and that the two aircraft in the fleet concept has been abandoned, can the minister say if the configuration of the aircraft for the two different roles that the single aircraft will have to play- the sovereignty role on the one hand, and the close support role in Europe on the other-will allow for interchangeability of aircraft, or will there be one aircraft with two distinct configurations?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I expect that they should be able to remain in one configuration for both roles. There may be a difference in the way they are armed, but they would be interchangeable in those roles. There would be room to have two different CF-18As or two different CF-16s. There may be some small adjustments in the roles, but not what one would consider different configurations.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my other question concerns the power plant. I understand that the power plant in the 16-if the designation of the F-16 is the same in Canadian terms as it is in United States terms-the power plant which is the F-100, I believe, of Pratt and Whitney, has run into some pretty scary problems. I wonder whether that has all been taken into account in the choice. I am not sure whether the 18A might not also have the same power plant, whether the minister is aware of these problems, and whether due allowance has been made for the work that is still to go into the F-100 engine, Pratt and Whitney, before it is ready to power even the American F-16.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that same engine is used to power the CF-16, the F-16 and the F-15. There are some teething problems as there generally are with new engines. Our
National Defence
team has looked into this very carefully and compared notes with other nations. Five of our allies are using this aircraft. I have personally spoken to colleagues in NATO and they are satisfied that this is a normal part of the development of a new engine that is taking place, and they are all confident that these problems will be overcome. Fortunately, if something arose that made that an invalid conclusion, it would be one of the things that our own evaluation team would follow extremely closely to make absolutely certain that we are not risking aircraft or, more important, Canadian pilots.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister said that five of our NATO allies are using the aircraft. Did he mean using them, or that they are on order by five other nations?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: They are on order by Norway, Denmark, the Netherlands, Belgium, and the United States.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the minister could clarify an answer that he gave to the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) earlier about the distribution of the acquisition when it takes place. Perhaps the minister will correct me if I am wrong in my reading of the statement, which is that the new allocations will be divided approximately 50 per cent to our NATO commitment and 50 per cent to our North American zone. That would lead me to the conclusion that we are increasing our commitment to NATO very substantially in terms of the number of aircraft we now have committed. I understand we are in the area of approximately 45 and are going to increase that to about 75 aircraft for our NATO role. Would the minister comment on that? If my figures are in error, perhaps he wishes to correct them.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think the hon. member's figures are in error but I think incorrect conclusions have been drawn from them. There are the 36 committed to central front in Baden. I believe there are 18 attrition and reserve aircraft and that works out to 54-I think I am right-that are there in the reserve role. They would have fly-over crews to support those. It may not be necessary with these new modern aircraft to maintain those additional aircraft in Germany because they all have fly-over capability-an unrefuelled fly-over capability-to the central front.
In addition, 24 are presently assigned to the north flank role. That is a fly-over role as well, from Bagotville and Cold Lake. The others are all in the North American defence role.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have concern to know how much study the minister and his officials have made in two areas of technology. The choice has been reduced to the two aircraft, the CF-16 and the CF-18A. My information is that in mock combat both of those aircraft have been very successful in eliminating each other in the air. In fact most new fighter aircraft have become so technologically advanced that they cancel each other when they get into combat. I would suspect the same would be true with Soviet aircraft, if we want to deal with the NATO question. Has the minister any Figures of the

November 23, 1978
National Defence
survival rate of these new proposed fighters in competition with themselves or other fighters? Will he table that? Perhaps he would respond to that, and I could have one more question.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: First of all, Mr. Speaker, they may cancel each other out. That is why we are only buying one kind, so that each will survive. I guess the likely combat is with Warsaw Pact forces. They are all highly sophisticated, but the survival rate has certainly been studied. I have the information in front of me but it would take some time to find it as it is a rather complex equation. I would be pleased to go over it with the hon. member at any time, however. Those are judgments that have been made and tested, computerized, and in some cases, I believe, in mock trials.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the minister gets my point in that question, which is that air cover that simply destroys itself in competition with the enemy is not air cover at all. My last question deals with the studies the minister has done on new weaponry, that is, heat seeking laser beam weaponry, which is the new technology in terms of support for ground forces, rather than fighter aircraft. Has the minister an assessment by his officials or his project team which deal s with the capacity of the new weapons using ground forces to eliminate fighter aircraft? Can he advise why it is that Canada seems to get in at the tail end of technology rather than at the beginning?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, those studies have been addressed. They are in my briefings and have merited consideration. I think this is one of the fortunate things in this buy, that we are phased in with the technology at a pretty reasonable stage-not so far in advance that we are getting into a "Never-Never Land" but sufficiently mature that we can make a wise judgment and at an early stage of the technical life of these aircraft that we have selected. They are at an early stage in their life cycle. None of them is actually in service per se yet. They are in the prototype and early production stages, but they have been fairly evaluated by others. One has been purchased by a number of nations, the other by the United States in significant quantities and is being looked at very seriously by others. I think we are at a rather good stage in the technology to have a high performance aircraft through the life cycle of 15 or 20 years.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I only have four more questions and, I might be able to put two of them together. I would like to ask the minister for the date of signing. Two statements were made by him today, one that we are making rapid progress to that end, and the other that it would be several months. I wonder if he could put an approximate number before the word months. Secondly, when does he expect that we will get the first plane out of this contract?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are proceeding as rapidly as we can to the date of signing in several months. That is the best way to describe it. To prepare the documentation, which is considerable, to sit down with the contractors will take one month or close to it for completion-it is close to completion,

but until the decision was made it could not be completed. It will likely be after Christmas before the vendors, the two contenders, have an opportunity to assess this. That is if they give up some of their Christmas recess for it. Our team should be able to sit down with the first group immediately after the New Year. This would be done by the same team sequentially, rather than at the same time, because it is necessary that the same people do the assessment so that we get the same qualitative judgment.
As I said the other day, I hope this will be all done by late spring. It is pretty difficult to be more definite than that because we want to make sure the negotiations are as exhaustive, as tough, and extensive as possible, and that we get the best buy and the best benefit from it.
Realistically one could only hope to look at April as a possible date of final completion. May or early June are real possibilities. I would not want to rush those and not get as good a deal, although I am anxious to see this purchase completed. I would rather have the best deal we can get by April. I would not want to put that additional pressure on the team to report when they are not satisfied they are ready. We will all be watching this closely. In so far as the first delivery is concerned, I believe the first delivery would be early in 1982. Depending on the number of aircraft we finally achieve, the rate is about two a month because of our cash flow requirements and abilities. This could take us to 1986 or 1987 before the final attrition aircraft are delivered.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that the minister on April 25, 1978, said that the government expected the first plane in 1981. Apparently there has been a slippage of one year, which is a considerable amount of slippage. Would the minister tell us if he is aware of any unrest or discontent in Air Command over the selection of these two planes? I have heard there is considerable discontent in Ottawa and several senior air force officers are most unhappy about the selection of the F-16 and F-18A.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be a little surprised if there was no criticism. I do not question the fact that airmen have favourites. I have spoken to many pilots throughout the system since I have been in this job and involved with new fighter aircraft. One does hear varying views. I know there are some concerns, some of which have been talked out and worked over by the Chief of Defence Staff, his senior people and everybody involved. There is full support of those people who have major responsibility. I believe what the hon. member is referring to, and I am sure it will be reflected in comment, is that the F-15 is a pretty hot aircraft. We know it is an excellent aircraft but so is the Tornado and the Tomcat.
I think in the main everybody realizes the need to have a sufficient number of aircraft in the total system and the capability which is realistic in terms of our assessment of the threat. More important and which must be taken into consideration here, is the question of the lifecycle cost. This is the
November 23, 1978

cost to keep those planes flying through their training system and exercises during their lifecycle. I have been apprised of the reservations each of the senior officers have had. The Chief of Defence Staff has kept me fully informed in this regard.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact the F-16 is something less than the world's greatest ground support plane, has the minister given consideration to a change of the role of our air arm in Germany?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: No, I do not think that will be necessary, Mr. Speaker. SACUER might decide. This will be discussed because of the new aircraft and the different set of capabilities, or a better capability really for the present role. These planes have considerable flexibility and may be used in a different role. That is not in the cards, and it is not necessary in the present considerations. However, that will develop perhaps as the strategic situation changes.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is it the minister's intention to bring down a white paper on defence in this session?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to bring one down on defence in this session. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss the defence policy concerns at much greater length which the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) and the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) have. The reason for not bringing down a white paper is not that I would not like to because there is work going on, but that it is not possible in this session due to the tremendous strain on resources in our department, particularly in the policy areas that have to be attributed to such a task.
It is not possible to do it in a short period of time and I would not want to see less than a first rate job done. I am sure the quality of people that we have would not want to attach themselves to anything they did not consider first rate. It is a matter of timing. In the circumstances, I think the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Rae) will agree that while thinking is taking place and input is going into what will ultimately be produced as a white paper, I just cannot put a date on it. It is keeping the ball bearings in everybody's two and one-half pound computer going.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sympathetic to the minister and his department's problem with ball bearings. I am concerned that if we are locking ourselves into a technology which will not become fully available until 1987, and which presumably will be in use until the year 2000-or who knows-it might be worth taking a little time. The minister said that he did not want to enter into something without a good deal. I put it to the minister and ask him to comment on it that if we are locking ourselves into a military strategy which will last, if the minister's plans take place, for at least 20 if not 25 years, would it not be a good idea to produce a white paper at the same time and allow members on all sides of the House, and the press at large, to discuss these matters before locking ourselves into these major decisions?
Order Paper Questions

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACQUISITION OF NEW FIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is certainly consistent with the priorities of the government, the assessment of military advisers in Canada and their joint considerations with NATO and NORAD. What we will buy is a capability with sufficient flexibility in growth that one can reasonably expect. This is always a difficulty with any major purpose. One would never buy anything if one would always wait for the next generation. That difficulty crops up every time something is put into production and it is taken from the drawing boards. Some engineers spend their lives keeping things on drawing boards which never get produced. They usually do not work for the same company for very long, but this happens. Sometimes you have to freeze drawings to get into production and get going. I think we are at the right end of the cycle with two flexible aircraft that could allow for any foreseeable change in role or strategy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure and honour to participate in this budget debate. For the past week we have heard a lot of blather by the official opposition, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), about Petro-Canada's purchase of Pacific Pete.
I submit that the hon. member for York-Simcoe and the Leader of the Opposition have misrepresented the facts on this matter. It is not only my opinion, but the opinion of the editorial board of the Toronto Sun. I wish to quote from its editorial dated November 22. As I indicated, I will quote directly from it. It is entitled "Clark Misleads on Petro-Canada", and I quote:
Conservative Leader Joe Clark is both naive and misleading in his obsessive attacks on Canada's national oil company, Petro-Canada. The company was set up in 1975 to give Canadians a stake in their own oil and gas industry, which is largely controlled by the big international oil companies.
Clark is naive when he says that Ottawa has all kinds of leverage which it could use to regulate the oil industry rather than acquiring its own national oil company.
Interestingly, Clark has never spelled out what kind of regulations he would apply to control the oil industry, perhaps because he's also promising to deregulate much of the Canadian economy and to cut the size of the civil service.
But to properly regulate something as complicated as the oil industry would require volumes of regulations and an army of civil servants, who would have to keep their eyes on every operation from the service station to exploration.
The country couldn't afford such an army. Even if it could, it would be difficult to ascertain the true situation. Canadians have only to recall how, based on industry-supplied forecasts and statistics, the National Energy Board thought there was a natural gas surplus when there was a shortage and how there was a shortage which turned out to be a surplus.
The last thing the international oil companies want is for the public to get an insider's view, which explains why the major oil companies in Canada have conducted such a strong campaign against Petro-Canada.
If Clark is naive in thinking he can control the oil industry through regulation, he is downright misleading when he suggests the $1.4 billion spent by Petro-Canada to acquire control of Pacific Petroleums Ltd. is an added burden on the taxpayer or that it represents reckless new spending by Ottawa.
Taxpayers' money is not being used by Petro-Canada to buy Pacific Petroleums. Instead, Canada's national oil company has borrowed the money from the Canadian banks and will be able to pay all the interest and principal from the future profits of Pacific Petroleums-and still have money left over for exploration and development. This is the same way takeovers are financed in the private sector.
The government's role is that of ultimate guarantor of the loan, but that doesn't cost it any money unless Pacific Petroleums, a highly profitable and oil-and-gas-rich company, should go bankrupt.
Clark is also wrong when he says, as he did this week in Parliament, that the money used to acquire Pacific Petroleums could have been used instead to help senior citizens or make it easier for Canadians to buy new homes.

November 23, 1978

There's a big difference between taking these worthwhile steps and giving Petro-Canada the green light to take over Pacific Petroleums. Taxpayers' money would have to be used to help the senior citizens and new homebuyers whereas there is no taxpayers' money used in the Petro-Canada acquisition.
In view of this editorial I submit that the hon. member for York-Simcoe and, particularly, the Leader of the Opposition, should withdraw the comments they have made which, not only in my opinion but in the opinion of the Toronto Sun editorial board, fail to reflect accurately the Petro-Can-Pacific Pete transaction.
The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), clearly and succinctly, put before the Canadian people the economic direction in which this country is to move within the ensuing year. It was a budget based not on political gimmickery but on sound principles of financial management; I submit a responsible budget. Generally, with the exception of the proponents of further deficit financing, the reaction has been favourable.
The reduction in the federal sales tax will help the consumer by slowing the rate of inflation. Other measures will help industry and induce them to invest. This creates permanent jobs in the long run. For example, Mr. Harvey Parliament, president of the Mining Association of British Columbia, is reported in the Express, November 20, 1978, as follows:
The next tax incentives improve the climate in the industry a lot. If there are mining properties that were thinking of going into production, but were teetering on the brink of making a decision, this may make them decide to go ahead.
As hon. members know, the proposal allows mining companies to write off 100 per cent of mining development costs, instead of the 30 per cent allowed up to now. Mining men and those in forestry are pleased with the budget's decision to allow a $100 deduction for every $300 spent on construction of townsites and the social assets that are involved. Similar favourable reaction has been received from these B.C. industries respecting the federal government's decision to maintain the write-offs for pollution equipment. The increase in the tax credit for new plant and equipment for expansion was also welcomed by industry in British Columbia.
Favourable reaction to this was given by the Employers' Council of British Columbia. They issued a press release on November 16, 1978, written by William Hamilton, President of the Employers' Council of British Columbia. I quote from their brief:
Given the constraints he faced, Chretien has produced a better budget than most business people expected. He had distributed a variety of tax changes between the personal sector and the business sector which will stimulate the economy. The western provinces will enjoy some particular benefits: He has re-emphasized the importance of our resource industries, especially mining, forestry, and petroleum, as a very basic source of Canadian economic growth.
We agree completely with the great emphasis Chretien placed on the responsibility of the private sector and individuals to pass on the benefits of this budget and to exercise personal restraint. In this way all Canadians will benefit from the measures announced which should provide a framework for further improving Canada's competitive position internationally.
We have some reservations about Mr. Chretien's forecast of inflation and economic growth which seems to us somewhat optimistic. However, we are encouraged by what seems to be the government's determination to exercise restraint and begin to build strength in the Canadian economy for the 1980s.
Unquestionably the budget was not expansionary. I submit to add to an already large deficit would have exacerbated our
The Budget-Mr. Lee
present economic situation. Canada is living in a tough, competitive world. Our unemployment rate is too high, especially among young Canadians. Prices are coming down, but not as fast as we would like. The Canadian dollar has declined in value.
Underlying these real economic challenges is the issue of national unity. We see a provincial government aiming to break up this country, to remove one province, a part of Canada, from this land of ours.
All hon. members have seen the deliberate, staged performances of Rene Levesque at first minister's conferences. We have heard all his blather about the federal government not helping the province of Quebec, that the federal government was not spending any money in Quebec. I could not believe it. Here was the premier of the province of Quebec saying his government does not receive any financial help from the federal government. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) corrected this fabrication. We are not only helping Quebec, but in many instances Quebec isn't even availing herself of the help we are offering.
Then we hear the cynics say the whole national unity issue is a government plot, a conspiracy to hold on to power. Well, I am not going to apologize for wanting to fight back when I see somebody, whether a pequiste or a western separatist, setting out deliberately or overtly to destroy my country. Neither does the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have to apologize for being determined to keep Canada strong and united.
There are cynics who say national unity is a government smokescreen to distract people from the economy. That's nonsense. I have talked to business people from the United States. They are not prepared to invest in a Canada that might fall apart. Of greater concern is the movement of Canadian business and industry from Quebec-I think, for example, of the Sun Life Corporation. It doesn't take a financial wizard to know that the unity crisis affects investment.
People in Vancouver East are concerned about national unity, but I know the issue can be pretty remote when one is unemployed and the cost of living isn't coming down fast enough. I know the people of Vancouver East are more concerned with the bread and butter issues, jobs and inflation. Even so, I don't have to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that unless we remain a strong country we won't have to worry about the economic challenges facing Canada.
Let's talk about the economy. Back in 1975 I spoke at the convention of my party and outlined Canada's economic problems as I saw them then. I should like to restate a few of the points I made because I think they are still applicable today. I began by talking about inflation, about what it was doing to Canada and to Canadians, about the way in which it disrupted financial planning by business and government, how it priced our goods out of world markets and created more unemployment. I talked about the way in which inflation undermines the position of those least able to protect themselves-pensioners and others living on fixed incomes. I said that the uncer-

November 23, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Lee
tainty caused by inflation provoked frustration, social unrest, and a distrust of private and public institutions. I said that it threatened the validity of collective bargaining and that it set labour up as a scapegoat for all our economic ills. I said that people were looking to the federal government for leadership and that, in my opinion, the federal government has fallen short of handling the economy as well as it could have done.
I called for a system of flexible wage and price controls. One month later, the federal government introduced them. Mr. Speaker, the anti-inflation program has worked. Controls were a success. When controls are phased out starting April 14 we shall all have to exercise the self-restraint which both labour and management have been telling government it would have to demonstrate once the controls are lifted. I, personally, do not anticipate any "bubble" of high wage demands and unwarranted price increases and, from what I have seen, this has not occurred. For one thing, Canadians are more aware than they were two and a half years ago of the impact which wage and price levels can have on our competitive position. There is a greater appreciation on the part of both labour and management that jobs and profits can be lost if our wages and prices get out of line with those of our competitors. We are more aware of the importance of economies of scale, entrepreneurial skills, and access to markets, as factors in our competitive situation.
I believe most Canadians feel that, despite its rough justice, the wage and price control program was about as fair as any such program could be. Workers, for example, are aware that while the guidelines may have restrained their wage demands, they also restrained prices. On balance, workers came out a little ahead of the game, which is better than one can say for their inflation experience in the two years before the controls program. The statistics support these calculations. Over the two-year period 1976-1977, wage increases under collective agreements monitored by the AIB amounted to roughly 18 per cent while the consumer price index increased by 15.9 per cent. This represents on average a gain in real wages of better than 2 per cent.
Another measure of the wage-price relationship is our experience with shares gross national product. The share of the GNP accorded to wages increased from 51.8 per cent in 1961 to 56.6 per cent in 1976, an increase of 5.1 percentage points. The wage share continued to rise, and in 1977 it was 57.2 per cent. It is wrong, therefore, to maintain as some still do, that the anti-inflation program was anti-labour. It is true that the guidelines placed restrictions around collective bargaining, but price increases have been restrained relatively more. The share of national income going to corporate profits has been fairly constant at 10.7 per cent to 11 per cent over the last decade, including the period under controls.
What has the government done about the bureaucracy? For two years there has been almost zero growth in the federal public service. The first ministers' conference agreed that compensation, wages and pensions to civil servants should follow those in the private sector. The first ministers also agreed to submit the growth of bureaucracy and regulations to

the Economic Council for study. A good start, but much more can be done. While there are many highly competent and highly dedicated people in the civil service, some civil servants are bilking the taxpayer by not giving a fair day's work for their pay. When I served on the sub-committee studying the penitentiary system I definitely saw this and I believe I could find the same thing in every federal department.
The federal government has lately regionalized many operations. Unfortunately, regionalism has come to mean little more than duplication of head office positions in the field without due concern for line and staff functions. I am gratified to see the government taking this aspect of the sub-committee's report on penitentiaries very seriously. What is required is not regionalism for the sake of regionalism, but real decentralization. Let me illustrate them with an example.
Some guards from the Kingston maximum security penitentiary went to the Ottawa airport to pick up prisoners. Because the plane was late, the guards went and got drunk. Fortunately, the RCMP officers accompanying the prisoners refused to turn the prisoners over to them. What was done about these guards? Their director wanted to fire them. The regional director wanted to fire them. Were they fired? No. Treasury Board officials advised they could only be suspended for a few days because of red tape. That is intolerable, Mr. Speaker.
We need to put the work ethic back into the public service. Managers should be able to hire, fire and transfer personnel more easily, and be able to offer cash incentives for good work. This is what we recommended for the penitentiary service, and I am sure the same is applicable to other departments. Managers, just as strongly as the public, want to get rid of the red tape that ties them up until they cannot function.
Now I should like to outline some of the things the government is doing to ease unemployment. First of all, why are so many people out of work? Is there something basically wrong with the system? The fact is the system is working pretty well considering that Canada is in the midst of an international economic recession. Last year the economy created more than
250,000	new jobs. In fact we had led the world in job creation and economic growth for years. Right now, though, two factors are coming together during a world-wide economic slowdown. We are still trying to absorb the last wave of the post-war baby boom into the labour force. At the same time, increasing numbers of women are leaving the home and entering the job market after being out of the work force for a few years. The result is a bulb in the labour force, and the job creating ability of the economy cannot keep up because our export and production performance is slowed down by world conditions.
Once the world recovers sufficiently from the present recession, the Canadian economy will pick up, and we will be able to bring unemployment down to normal levels. In the meantime the federal government is providing a gradual stimulus to production and investment, creating jobs directly and provid-
November 23, 1978

ing training and experience to young people so that they will be employable workers when the economy has recovered.
Let us look at the record. First, there have been income tax reductions amounting to $2 billion so that we can stimulate consumer demand.
Second, there has been a $900 million cut in corporate taxes to encourage private enterprise to invest and create jobs.
Third, more than $1 billion has been spent on direct job-creation programs. Since 1974 Vancouver East has received $6,751,499 under the Local Initiatives Program, the Canada Works Program and the Young Canada Works Program, and 1,278 jobs have been created.
Fourth, the experimental $100 million employment tax credit program will encourage the private sector to create more permanent jobs.
Fifth, the Alcan pipeline legislation will create 100,000 man-years of employment. For British Columbia a total of 1,800 man-years will be required from 1981 to 1982 to construct the pipeline. At peak periods the work force will reach 1,750 people.
Sixth, the $150 million salmon enhancement program for British Columbia will help ensure adequate stocks of this natural resource and double the existing $200 million wholesale value catch.
Seventh, the 200-mile economic zone for coastal provinces will be a distinct advantage to the British Columbia fishing industry. Presently I am working with the port of Vancouver to establish better facilities for fish processors.
Eighth, a government subsidized loan of $1.5 million has been made to establish a proper drydock facility in the port of Vancouver.
Ninth, of a $117 million expenditure for West Coast ports $40 million was spent on the new Vanterm container facility and $26 million on Lynterm, the sister facility of Vanterm, which is designed for bulk loading.
Tenth, there has been a commitment by the federal government to build a new federal building in Vancouver. Unquestionably, that will pick up the slack in the construction trade, which is suffering 30 per cent to 40 per cent unemployment. It will create 250,000 man-days of work.
Eleventh, a $50 million tourist agreement has just been signed with the British Columbia government.
Twelfth, there is a $186 million agreement for agricultural and industrial incentives under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
I would like to say a few words about western alienation. There is a myth that somehow we in the west are bankrolling the rest of the country. Lately this myth has attached itself to the equalization policy, under which all taxpayers in Canada share equally in the services for which their taxes pay. One sometimes gets the impression that the people who believe this myth think that bags of money are being loaded on to planes in Vancouver, Calgary and Edmonton so that they can be dropped from the skies on to Quebec and the maritime prov-
The Budget-Mr. Lee
inces. The fact is that Canada is one country, and we all contribute to the well-being of all Canadians. Quebeckers and maritimers pay taxes just as Albertans and British Columbians do, and the federal income tax rate is the same wherever we live.
I suspect that there is a certain amount of prejudice behind the myth that the west is paying for the east. The complaint is always about how much Quebec receives in equalization payments. We never hear people complaining about how much the federal government gives in equalization payments to Saskatchewan and Manitoba, or even Newfoundland. The other half of the myth is the false assertion that the federal government has not done anything good for the west. This old chestnut is still being kicked around, despite the fact that we need only pick up a newspaper to see how the west has benefited from confederation.
Let us look at some of the things which have been done by the federal government in the west. The government has recognized that the economic base of western Canada must be widened. That is why massive amounts of federal money and effort have gone into saving the Syncrude development of the Alberta tar sands.
The federal government has recognized that Canada's old trade patterns, based on trans-Atlantic trading, are outdated. That is why Ottawa has been pulling out all the stops to boost trade with Japan and other Pacific Rim countries which will buy our products. I note that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) is in the House. He just returned from a trip to Pacific Rim countries with that very object in mind.
Ottawa has recognized that the decision-making, employment, and purchasing powers of the federal government should apply outside central Canada. That is why the mint was moved to Winnipeg. That is why a taxation data center is being opened in Surrey, British Columbia, to handle all tax returns from British Columbia and Yukon. That is why the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has been decentralized all over this country.
Let us consider the massive federal assistance which will be needed to make development of the northeast coal deposits in British Columbia a major shot in the arm to the provincial economy. A $10 million study into environmental, social, engineering and transportation aspects of coal development has been initiated as a result of a federal-provincial agreement. Let us consider the millions of dollars in federal subsidies which will support coastal transportation communities on the north coast.
The main contribution to British Columbia which the federal government makes is in the area of federal-provincial transfer payments. From 1975 to 1978 the federal government gave British Columbia more than $3 billion in federal transfer payments. That Figure includes direct federal payments to individuals through family allowances, old age pensions and veterans' benefits. Apart from that $3 billion blockbuster, the federal government pours hundreds of millions into the British

November 23, 1978
Adjournment Motion
Columbia economy every year to keep normal government operations going.
The people who work in local Manpower offices, the Federal Business Development Bank, the Post Office, immigration offices and so forth, are British Columbians whose salaries are being paid out of the taxes which all Canadians pay to the federal Department of National Revenue.
In 1975 and 1976 the Post Office spent more than $95 million in British Columbia. Transport Canada spent more than $44 million, and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce spent $10 million. The Department of Supply and Services, which purchases all the equipment and goods which the federal government uses in its operations-from paper clips to trucks-spent more than $146 million. Just think how many suppliers of government contracts keep their businesses alive because they have the federal government as one of their customers. Just think how much that means to the economy of British Columbia.
Unfortunately the total amount of federal spending in my province is unknown. No one has ever worked that figure out because our nationhood is not based on a balance sheet.
Before I finish, there is one other topic I wish to spend a few moments discussing, and again I draw attention to the fact that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is in the House. In the throne speech debate back in 1976 I spoke about the desire of western Canada for freer trade. With the government's decision to impose quotas on shoes and textiles I submit that the government is moving away from its commitment to freer trade. Protectionism costs Canadians from coast to coast money. We are all consumers, whether we live west of the Rockies or east of the Ottawa River. If we do away with import duties, we will all be better off from an economic point of view.
