speechtext:
It is amusing, Mr. Speaker, to witness this government in its last gasping death throws. The backbenchers are handing out statistics to show Canadians, who know otherwise, that things are very good economically. It reminds me of Louis XIV who was about to disappear when the minions were handing him his towel as he jumped out of the shower. Such was the speech the hon. member just made. In fact he made quite a good speech but I think it was more or less prepared for the hustings in the election which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) did not have the guts to call. I think that my analogy of Louis XIV is accurate in terms of the statistics the hon. member was quoting.
There was a headline in the press today that the present Auditor General does not like horror stories. Although he may not like them, and although we on this side of the House have only had a few hours to study his report, already the horror stories are coming out. There are plenty of them in this Auditor General's report, as in the reports of other auditor generals that have been produced since this government has taken power.
We on this side of the House have only had a little time to study the general meaning of the report, but there is one comment in the report which I would like to refer to all hon. members. It says that there are no criteria in place guiding the decision-making powers on over $10 billion for capital projects in place for 1977-78, and that competitive bidding practices are not in place over a high percentage of this. This confirms my view that this government is the most patronage ridden government this country has had since Confederation. I have said this all along, and I have been accused of being too partisan, but now the Auditor General is saying it.
The Auditor General also says that we are now moving into an era of comprehensive audit, with emphasis on special procedures in cost effectiveness, designed to change the attitudes of those managing the systems because as it appears now the quality of management leaves much to be desired. There is no myth about who is responsible for this; it is the government. The only thing wrong with this country is the mismanagement of the present government. A little kid in my riding last week told me that this government is going to go out like a bullet in the next election.
The Auditor General also said that in his opinion there was widespread lack of due regard for economy and efficiency in the operation of the government, and that inadequate attention
November 23, 1978

is being given to programs costing millions of dollars and whether they are accomplishing what parliament intended. This report, together with reports of previous auditors general, and the views of millions of Canadians confirm that this government is the most wasteful government since confederation and is mismanaging our economy as no other government has mismanaged it since confederation.
In looking through chapter three of the Auditor General's report with regard to airports, the Auditor General virtually suggested that he was going to withhold what is referred to in the private sector, as the normal time of auditing certification. In other words, he almost wanted to disown himself from the disaster. What is implicit in his comments is that he is withholding normal auditing practice certifications. It is the first time that this sort of thing has happened in any Auditor General's report in my time here in the House of Commons.
If this government took as serious the reports of the auditors general over the last number of years-and I know that my hon. friends to the left will support me on this-we could have saved millions and billions of dollars and channeled them into vital social and welfare programs.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, we are of course in agreement with some proposals in last week's budget including, as the hon. member for Ottawa-Centre (Mr. de Cotret) would have clearly indicated yesterday afternoon, the reduction from 12 per cent to 9 per cent in the federal sales tax as it affects a number of manufactured goods.
However I would have to put a number of questions at this point to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). These questions are clear and simple. I would like to ask this to the minister: What proposals does your budget include to help low income people, the poor? What proposals does your budget include to help small businessmen, solve unemployment, stimulate the economy, or eliminate economic stagnation? And here is another question of significance to the Auditor General: To control budget deficits, to control inflation, what proposals are there? This is another question I am putting to the Minister of Finance.
Mr. Speaker, the answers are quite obvious. This budget means no real growth for the economy, and an analysis of the proposals put forward by the minister clearly shows that unfortunately we will have more unemployment in the future, no improvements in the inflation rate and a larger budget deficit.
In his speech, the minister discussed the outlook for the future. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I did not listen very closely because the minister's forecasts have always been proved wrong. The public and the House both lost confidence in the minister forecasts. And I repeat, the Canadian people have lost all confidence in the government.
Mir. Breau: No, they did not!

speechtext:
Like many Canadians I said to myself a number of months ago, "Why did Mr. Goldfarb"-I mean the right hon. Prime Minister-"not call an election?" I do not think that I am known on Parliament Hill as being a hidebound traditionalist, but there is one tradition that has been here a long time, and that is that we are supposed to have an election every four years in this country. Since he did not call the election Canadians assumed that the Prime Minister must have something, apart from civil war in Quebec, very big in mind. He gave no explanation of why he was not calling an election.
We all then awaited the throne speech. In my 20 years on Parliament Hill, the last throne speech was the worst. I am not kidding myself, but when we were in power, although the throne speeches may have been a little vague, they at least had some meat to them. After hearing the throne speech and realizing there was nothing in it, I thought that we should be patient and wait for the government's legislative package. Once again there was nothing. Perhaps the hon. ministers opposite have isolated themselves in their ivory towers in their death throes, because there was not one single thing.
The Prime Minister said that he had something big in mind, but in the view of the Canadian people it was certainly not in the throne speech or in the legislative package which has been presented to parliament. And we are almost at Christmas time. But no matter, Mr. Speaker, even if he did present something relatively big now, it would be far too late for anything that may happen this winter, so we can rule out anything happening in terms of meaningful legislation.
Now we have this budget, Mr. Speaker. When I was a parliamentary secretary many years ago with the minister of finance, we regarded a budget as a major document which told the Canadian people where we had come from and where we were going. It was a major document that showed the Canadian people the economic direction and economic policy of the government of the day. By bringing down three budgets in one year the federal government has virtually undermined the credibility of a budget. I challenge the government opposite to go to the Canadian people on this budget, on their legislative package, and on their throne speech. I say there is not one single item that authorizes the Prime Minister to go beyond the traditional mandate for calling an election.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, budgets are supposed to be a grand design that indicates government policy to the Canadian people. I admit that because of the gross economic mismanagement of the worst government we have had since Confederation, the poor Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has been placed in a hopeless pickle. He had two alternatives. One was to dare to go ahead with a bold new design and cut new ground; the other was to work within the confines of the narrow parameters set out for him by this awful government. He chose the latter, and what we got was tinkering and lack of vision.

November 23, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Grafftey
I ask, is that what has kept parliament going on? I hope not. The only possible excuse, having seen the government's budget, its throne speech, and its legislative package, is this. The Prime Minister used to be an NDPer in Quebec but he took over the Liberal party. As a result, there now exists this Liberal disease, which is that hon. members opposite have some divine right to continue to rule this country, even when they have brought this country to its economic knees. This parliament has been prolonged not for the survival of Canada but for the survival of the Liberal party. They keep underlining day after day and year after year this divine right to govern this country, even after the years of gross economic mismanagement.
Just what do we have, Mr. Speaker, after ten years of this government? Unimaginable budgetary deficits, record unemployment, inflation, the lowest dollar relationship to the United States dollar since confederation, and, last but not least, record interest rates that hurt most of all Canadians of low income. These are the very people I have always said members on both sides of the House are here to protect. These are the very people who have been shafted most by the gross economic mismanagement of this government. Certainly they have been shafted the most by high interest rates.
I do not care what statistics the minions of the Prime Minister hand him as he sits in his ivory tower; in the last ten years more and more Canadians have fallen below the poverty line because of Ottawa's foolhardy policies. Gathered in cabinet on the opposite side of the House is the worst collection of economic illiterates that this country has ever seen. With their record, Mr. Speaker, how can they presume to prolong this parliament over and above the traditional mandate? But it will not be long, Mr. Speaker. You bet it will not be long. However, we on this side of the House have to look at you guys over there for another winter.

They may be laughing now, Mr. Speaker, but they will not be laughing when their quarterback finally calls the election.
I am glad to see that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) is in the House this afternoon because I want to talk about our attitude to the proposed purchase of Pacific Petroleums. Certainly their attitude with regard to the purchase of Nordair and Pacific Petroleums underlines how completely even the so-called free enterprise businessmen in the cabinet have lost touch with private sector realities.
The minister of energy proposed to give us a lecture the other day on how companies get finance. I am quite well aware, I will tell the minister, as is the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), of how Petro-Canada, with the aid of the chartered banks, proposes to take over Pacific Petroleums. Like hon. members opposite, I too have read the details of the proposed chartered bank financing of this takeover. I am as aware as the government of how it is proposed to buy Nordair. The government may have competely lost touch with reality somewhere along the line, but although they have diddled the books enough in terms of public accounting, they cannot diddle this book.
I had Frank Scott, a constitutional law expert, as my professor at McGill, and compared to him the lectures that I have had from members on the other side of the House on constitutional law, and on varying degrees of governmental responsibility for actions taken in the name of the Crown, have been pretty bad. Nevertheless, having gone through the plethora of combinations of argument, the fact is that somewhere down the line the government will indirectly incur a liability for taking over Pacific Petroleums and Nordair.
I ask the minister of energy to state yes or no a little more clearly than he has in the past just what is the position. I do not buy the argument that the government can satisfy its quasi-doctrinaire propensities for cutting back because it has an ex-NDPer who took over the Liberal party as a short-term prime minister. That side of the House has the worst of both worlds-the worst of the free enterprise world and the worst of the socialist world. It is on that basis of lack of principle that the government has brought this country to its economic knees.

He has only been hitting about .125 since he has been on the other side of the House.
Having said that, I would say to the ministry opposite that in purchasing Nordair and Pacific Petroleums Ltd., somewhere down the line they will be incurring indebtedness, indirectly. I think it is a pretty poor show during a week when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is in Toronto telling her provincial counterparts that we will cut back on health resource programs, health research and bloc
November 23, 1978

funding of social services at the community level, that the government, to satisfy its quasi-doctrinaire urges, purchases Pacific Petroleums Ltd. and Nordair.
I am a little surprised at my colleagues to the left. I usually have a great deal of honest admiration for their spokesman on energy, but I was a little surprised the other day that he supported this move which involves billions of dollars at the same time as we are cutting back on health and welfare services and the like. They, too, lose their sense of reality when they get caught up with their doctrinaire urges, which I submit are more realistic for a bygone age.
This week and last week the Minister of Finance announced the unilateral cutback of programs affecting the provinces. The Prime Minister said this is because of fiscal restraint. I reiterate that in the case of bloc funding of social services at the community level not only the question of money was involved but also a whole new system that the federal and provincial ministers of welfare had worked out with the provinces over a long period. Holus-bolus, unilaterally, the Minister of Finance cancelled the programs. Apart from considerations of restraint, is this the way to deal with the provinces? I suggest that when programs like that are cancelled unilaterally, the waste of money is incredible.
Let me be more specific about the government's plans for cutting back on the health resources fund, Mr. Speaker. The position of this party on restraint is very clear. I am sure I am representing the party when I say we must be selective. Very often Treasury Board moves into certain programs like a bull in a china shop, without understanding the implications, and so the results are incredible.
If there is one thing I have some knowledge of it is the health resources fund. It was a multi-million dollar fund put in place not only to organize community health services, to humanize and make more decent the delivery of health care services, but also one of the centrifugal aspects of the fund was to rationalize costs. One of the means of doing this was to train paramedical people to take the place of high cost doctors, by building units less expensive than the curative community hospitals, and by helping research. In the name of restraint, however, the government went hog-wild. Treasury Board, with no knowledge of the centrifugal aspect of this program apart from its human dimensions, just cut costs. They went in to cancel and cut. I maintain that by cutting in the area of health resources you waste rather than save.
I want to lay another myth to rest, Mr. Speaker. Time and time again in past weeks the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and his party have put forward propositions vis-a-vis local tax deductions for housing. With an almost Pavlovian dog reaction, the government said this was for the rich and not for the poor. I think we have laid to rest the argument that not all homeowners with young families and sizeable mortgages can automatically be classified as rich. Apart from that, however, it is quite a fallacious argument.
The benefit we want for homeowners is a benefit that lessees have been getting indirectly for years. The owner of buildings, houses and condominiums, rents them and directly or indirect-

ly has been able to benefit from the tax provision that we provided for homeowners in the past. The benefits that we are proposing for future homeowners are benefits that have largely been enjoyed by lessees in the past.
Hon. members opposite sneer at our proposal. It is not just an ad hoc proposal like so many made by the government but is one that goes to the heart of the principles and philosophy of this party. As we go to victory at the next election, we say that we believe that democracy is well served, in the best sense of the word, when the individual citizen has an ownership stake in the country. Unlike the socialists and the Liberals, holding on to their doctrinaire ideas which were more relevant in the thirties than today, we believe that government has a role to play in encouraging what I call a property-owning-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to take part in this debate to state openly and publicly that I fully agree with the responsible approach of the government with regard to the financial and economic management of our country. Mr. Speaker, the government could easily have taken advantage of this budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) to pander to the tastes of the people. On the other hand, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) could easily have abstained from making the decisions which required the support and co-operation of the Canadian people, but he chose to do so, because we know that in spite of all the speeches made by members opposite and all the half-truths spread by them, the Canadian people prefer a government which assumes its responsibilities and tells the truth.
Mr. Speaker, the best proof given by the government that it intends to run this country in a responsible fashion and to seriously curb its spending has been its decision to come to grips with a program which was indeed very popular in some quarters but gave rise to abuses and excesses that could no longer be tolerated, namely, the unemployment insurance program.
As a result of the decisions taken by the government to reduce and make more stringent the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act covering benefits and the eligibility of Canadians, Mr. Speaker, from now till the end of the current taxation year we will save $150 million while for 1979-80 we will save some $580 million and for the following year almost $1 billion by making the unemployment insurance scheme much more restrictive.

speechtext:
The member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) will have the opportunity to speak in due time, Mr. Speaker. He makes me laugh because a survey made by Ottawa University Professor Bodkin shows that the generosity of the government with its unemployment insurance policy has created an artificial unemployment of at least 2 per cent so that the real unemployment rate in our country must be about 6 to 6.5 per cent. Indeed, what happened is that the original intent of the unemployment insurance scheme has been distorted. This is not an insurance against unemployment any more, Mr. Speak-
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
er; it has become a social welfare measure which too many Canadians take advantage of as soon as they meet the legal requirements. Mr. Speaker, I think it is time that the government thought about those who work, who pay taxes, who get up in the morning and have the guts to go out and earn a living and I think the government is doing just that. Of course, the present economic situation makes it impossible for some of us who really want to work to find jobs and we deplore that fact. The government does not want to penalize these people anyway, but to punish those who found a way to systematically take advantage of the generosity of our program.
Mr. Speaker, one of the big deceptions I had in recent weeks or even months was to hear some ministers of the Quebec government mislead Quebeckers by pretending that the federal budget restrictions were aimed first and foremost at jeopardizing the interests of the province of Quebec, and yet they had already recognized the advisability and necessity for the federal government to reduce its spending in some very specific fields. For example, using an analogy, the finance minister said that it was a bit like someone clearing the snow in his driveway by shovelling it over to his neighbour's entrance. I think the Quebec finance minister could have told the population that those people who will no longer be eligible for unemployment insurance because of the new requirements in the law will in some cases get welfare benefits of which, Mr. Speaker, 50 per cent are financed by the federal government under the Canada Assistance Plan.
I would add, Mr. Speaker, that in any event fewer than 10 per cent of those who will no longer be eligible for unemployment insurance will become recipients of welfare benefits because in several cases they are young people still living at home with their parents, and their parents can support them. In some cases it is a man or a woman whose spouse is working and earning an adequate income. Mr. Speaker, when I was a student, I never thought about that, it never occurred to me that by working so many weeks I could have applied for unemployment insurance. Not only me but also my fellow students. People with whom I used to study managed to work during summer. We were saving enough money and then were studying for eight, nine or ten months at the university with the modest amount of money we had managed to save.
Mr. Speaker, I was also deeply disappointed to hear in the last few months a minister in the Quebec government, the Minister of Industry and Commerce, denounce throughout Quebec the position of the federal government on the Ford matter. He stated on several occasions that the federal government prejudiced Quebec's interests by allowing Ford Motors to build their plant in Ontario. Mr. Speaker, the people in Quebec should know that the choice was not between Quebec and Ontario. The choice was between an investment by Ford Motors in the state of Ohio, in the United States, or an investment in the Windsor area, in Ontario.

But such decisions are not made by governments finally but by business leaders who think in terms of economic profitability.
Mr. Speaker, I am a member of a party which is very tolerant, and for that reason, I feel well at ease to bring that matter to the attention of the House, and I am glad to note that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) is now in the House because it is a matter which I know is of great interest to him. What I have in mind, Mr. Speaker, is the issue concerning the heavy water plant in Laprade, Quebec.
Strictly speaking, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the arguments raised by the minister make a lot of sense because there is no point in building a heavy water plant if, on the one hand, there is already overproduction of heavy water in Canada as a whole and if, on the other hand, the cost to Quebec consumers is going to be higher if they are supplied by the heavy water plant which could be built in Laprade. However, Mr. Speaker, I wonder why the federal government signed that agreement earlier this year. I suppose the reasons we have been bringing forward since last August were already as good in January and February.
Mr. Speaker, rigorously and objectively speaking we are certainly right but I think the minister should understand the significant political dimension of that matter. The minister should understand that the credibility of the federal government is at stake in the province of Quebec and that its credibility is very important given the important debates now taking place and given the major decisions that Quebeckers will have to make in the coming months. I think there is a symbol here and it would therefore be very important to reconsider the entire matter. Indeed, 1,500 jobs are at stake and I think that it is imperative that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources make a proposal to the government of Quebec. What he should do is offer a compensation such as the extension of the natural gas pipeline to the east or simply accept to give further action to the agreement already signed because what is noticeable for people is that an agreement has been signed and that we withdraw unilaterally from it now.
Mr. Speaker, the government budget restrictions cannot be prejudicial to Quebec's interests. It is easy to prove, regardless of what the Quebec government may say. Let us take, for example, the revision of family allowances. In 1979, Mr. Speaker, this change, which will benefit low income families
The Budget-Mr. Duclos and require of the more privileged that they forgo $5 a month for each child, means, as far as Quebec is concerned, an additional injection of $60 million during the coming year.
Also, I should like to take this opportunity to stress that as far as the riding of Montmorency-which I have the honour to represent here-is concerned, the net result of this measure will be an additional 2.7 million in family allowances. And if we add to that old age security, a sector where the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has performed a feat in spite of budgetary restraints, has managed to raise almost $300 million, of which $82 million will go directly to Quebec, I wonder, Mr. Speaker, how one can say that this government do not serve the interests of Quebeckers.

Mr. Speaker, a few weeks ago, we studied Bill C-5, a measure which specifically provided for this $20 a month increase per household for senior citizens, and also a six-month extension of the spouse allowance to help the spouse who loses his or her partner to death to face the situation more easily. Naturally it is easy to say that something is not enough. I say, Mr. Speaker, it is a step in the right direction. I find that rather strange. I remember the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) expressing pity for the fate of the women and the men who, having lost their spouse, would also lose their pension. I found that strange, that taken individually, those hon. members of the opposition may be sincere; I am willing to trust them. But, Mr. Speaker, they should realize that their worst ennemy, if they are really sincere, is their party, taken as a whole, which constantly and indirectly, with great subtlety, attacks the social policies of the government, insinuating that it does too much for the people. However, I believe that the government could spend a bit more than it does now so that eventually old age pensions would be available at the age of 60. One of the beneficial results of such an action, Mr. Speaker, would be to free jobs for our young people who want to work, and there are some young people who want to work, Mr. Speaker. There are a number of spongers in our society, but I believe that most young people want to work, to have an interesting job and to be motivated.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to discuss the attitude of our friends opposite concerning the economic situation of Canada as a whole. On the one hand, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) asks for a considerable reduction in our deficit. This is not a bad idea; I believe that it is a valid objective, Mr. Speaker. On the other hand, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) maintains that we must reduce taxes. It would not be a bad idea to reduce our deficit and reduce taxes. However, I believe that this would entail lower expenditures.
When discussing income tax reduction, Mr. Speaker, we are immediately reminded of the proposition made by the Leader of the Opposition who would have municipal taxes and mortgage interests made deductible from the taxable income of the taxpayers.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that if we think about it for one second we see this is a totally irresponsible proposition. Mr. Speaker, it is known for instance that after four years- because this scheme would cover a four-year period-the
federal government would lose at least $2 billion in fiscal revenues, not to mention the $750 million lost by the provinces which, of course, would not collect these revenues. Besides, I would like to point out the interesting fact that we are very often blamed for not consulting the provinces when we implement various policies. Mr. Speaker, in an area closely related to provincial taxation, I do not believe that the Leader of the Opposition bothered to consult very many provinces, I believe that in future he should not teach us too many lessons in this respect. And besides, if the home owners who have completely paid off their mortgage or have paid part of it were to decide-as they would probably do because nobody is stupid enough not to grab such and opportunity-to refinance completely their house, we cannot even project the possible costs, the taxes that might be lost by the government.
Mr. Speaker, the effects would be first an increase in mortgage interest rates. When money goes to the mortgage market, there are less funds available for industrial development, mining development and the various economic developments required by our country. Mr. Speaker, with the increase in interest rates, municipal financing would be much more costly, and in order to meet their responsibilities, municipalities would have to increase property taxes, thus offsetting the benefits that taxpayers might derive from the proposal made by the Leader of the Opposition. Mr. Speaker, it is also a socially unfair measure as, considering the progressive nature of tax rates in Canada, savings would increase with higher taxable incomes.
Furthermore, it is obvious that people with luxury homes, with the most expensive residences, will take advantage of the $5,000 maximum provided by the proposal of the official opposition leader: the owners of small bungalows would not get the maximum, but rather the people who are able to pay for luxury homes and with a high standard of living. Mr. Speaker, I do not consider this as a socially equitable policy and I am prepared, in my riding, to defend the government's position on that issue and to attack the irresponsibility of the opposition party. Mr. Speaker, I know that it is not enough to criticize. For my part, when I criticize a proposal made by my political opponents, I like to propose an alternative. The aim in my view should be to help homeowners who really need this help, while maintaining a responsible fiscal and budget policy. One proposal I would have in that respect would be to allow small homeowners to deduct up to $1,000 from taxable income, depending on how much deduction they claimed for interests and dividends because, as you know, there is a maximum $1,000 exemption for dividends and interests.
Mr. Speaker, this would help small homeowners and we know that thousands can barely pay their mortgages and taxes, and are unable to save. They would use the maximum $1,000 deduction.
Mr. Speaker, the more affluent homeowners, those already receiving dividends and interests in excess of $1,000 could not benefit, and rightly so. Such a policy would be socially fair,

because the government's first priority is to care for the small in society.
Mr. Speaker, an exemption is also needed for the aged. We are aware that a number of old age pensioners essentially live off their savings, they receive dividends and interests, so they could be allowed a deduction at the uniform and flat rate of $1,000. The advantage in that proposal, Mr. Speaker, is that we know the cost. It would be roughly $300 million. This might be implemented on a gradual basis, to conform with current economic and financial conditions, but such should be the goal. As I said, Mr. Speaker, deficit reduction is good. Income tax reductions I support. But the opposition should be a little more specific when time comes to talk about spending cuts. One hears relatively few suggestions. You know, Mr. Speaker, it is not hard, to reduce a deficit there are not very many ways of going about it. Either you reduce spending or you increase taxes, or a combination of both. There are no alternatives. If you reduce taxes, you essentially have to reduce spending. I noted that the Progressive Conservatives are even prepared to contradict themselves, are so power hungry that they are prepared to make the worst contradictions, and they think that Canadians are going to fall for that farce. You can fool all people from time to time, you can fool some people all the time but you cannot fool all people all the time. I think it is time that the opposition dropped their masks, that they showed their real face. The time for truth has come in this country. I challenge the Progressive Conservatives to present a budget. It could be called the budget of the year I of the Progressive Conservative party. A budget. We are going to be waiting for that. I ask them questions. Present that budget and answer the following questions: What would be the size of the deficit? How and by how much would taxes be reduced, by how much and by cutting into what expenditures, cutting into what programs would spending be reduced? There are elementary principles which should not be forgotten. To achieve both a deficit and tax reduction expenditures must be curtailed more so than taxes. November 23, 1978
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
Mr. Speaker, once again this House has to deal with one of these quarterly interventions by the Minister of Finance in the shaping of our economic policy.
Those numerous and awkward efforts to steer to the right and then to the left prove only one thing-the glaring incompetence of the Minister of Finance. If he had seen right last spring, we would not have to discuss once again such important economic issues. Had the minister listened to advice from the opposition, because we gave him good opinions and also those of experts, Canada would now be on the road to economic recovery. The Canadian dollar would be in a stable position and we would have registered real success against inflation.
In light of past efforts and if I consider those failures which have marked all those interventions last year, this budget will fall far short of the lofty goals at which the minister is so confidently aiming. However, as the minister is crossing a political desert, he can do nothing but whistle to recover his morale while he is spending our money. Economists agree on one point: this budget will fail to stimulate the economy and appreciably cut down unemployment. On the contrary, it is evident that the Minister of Finance has decided to use unemployment as his principal instrument to fight desperately an ever threatening inflation.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, thousands of Canadian workers are going to pay for the mistakes, the foolishness and the maladministration of this government. While attempting to deceive us by talking about expenditure cutbacks, the minister is in fact increasing federal spending. Mr. Speaker, under the present government, words have lost their real meaning and only the minister has the nerve to pretend that we will reduce our spending by increasing them. Our party proposes longterm budgeting-preferably five years-but the minister prefers to table a hold-the-line budget, desperately hoping that the situation will improve as if by magic and that the government will not be defeated in the months to come.
Mr. Speaker, in the hands of this government, the budget is no longer an instrument of economic policy but simply a ploy of electoral propaganda. It is in fact one of the reasons why we heard so many economic statements this year. And in spite of a few welcomed initiatives, the same applies to the last budget. Indeed, a deficit of at least $12 billion does nothing to restore confidence among business circles nor does it strenghten our dollar on international markets. It is not the first time the Minister of Finance is engaged in double talk. While bragging about the merits of devaluating the dollar, he is increasing its value by putting the interest rates to an unprecedented level which will only worsen the stagnation of our economy. The so-called benefits of a decrease in the value of the dollar will be wiped off for the consumer by an increase in financing costs and economic activities. It is as if the minister was trying to save a drowning man he has just thrown in the lake with a milestone around his neck or as if somebody was feeling compelled to sell his stove to buy wood. In my view, this is

more or less the attitude of the Minister of Finance. Our dollar is likely to go on sinking straight to the bottom as it has been doing since the minister assumed his present portfolio. Mr. Speaker, I think I am hearing some strange noises, therefore I hope to continue at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I will continue my speech. I readily admit that tax exemptions for some industries are very commendable indeed. My only regret is that they have not been granted earlier, as we in the Progressive Conservative party have been advocating it for a long time, especially in the
November 23, 1978

case of resource industries. The reduction of the federal sales tax from 12 per cent to 9 per cent is definitely a step in the right direction, but it is not addressed to the heart of the problem of the costs that overburden the Canadian manufacturing industry. Moreover, it is not entirely sure that the benefits of the operation will be fully passed on to consumers. The indexing of the basic exemption for personal income tax purposes will at the most enable a taxpayer to keep his purchasing power.
The tax credit granted for employment expenses which is raised from $250 to a limit of $500 seems generous at first sight, but it is really quite small for workers and will not fully compensate for the increase in transportation costs and the price of tools. I sincerely regret that the minister has found necessary to increase the airport tax by 15 per cent. There is no clearer evidence of the wealthy bourgeois mentality which characterizes this government than this tax increase the principal victims of which will be the passengers with little or no means. Air travel in this country is not for the exclusive use of the rich businessmen and vacationers .
The airplane is a vital means of transportation in the outlying areas of Canada, be it in the North or in regions where other means of transportation are not available, or on the many islands off our coasts. I am especially referring, as far as my province is concerned, to the people of the Magdalen Islands among others, who can reach the mainland by plane only and who are not exactly among the richest citizens of our country. I am also referring to the workers of the north coast and of new Quebec who once in a while want to visit their families in the Gaspe peninsula. I am also thinking about the Indians and the people working on the James Bay project whose transportation expenses will go up again. And what about the people of Prince Edward Island, of Newfoundland, of the Northwest Territories or of the northern parts of all our provinces? What about all the Canadians who are scattered all over the country and who have no other means of transportation but the airplane to get together at Christmas time or for the funerals of one of their relatives? I am thinking of those new Canadians of less than modest means who may want to go back home, to the old country, for one last time. The government would not have acted otherwise even if they had actually wanted to get at the most needy of Canadians.
I also regret that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has not seen fit to adopt our party's recommendations regarding deductibility of mortgage interests and property taxes on a homeowner's principal residence. This measure, which would be of immense benefit to our economy in several industrial sectors, will be one of the Progressive Conservative party's top priorities after the Canadians have given us the mandate to govern this country. And since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) likes to link the economic problem with that of national unity, I do not think that it is irrelevant for me to say a word about the pitiful and deplorable speech given over the week-
77! e Budget-Mr. La Salle
end by the head of this government before the Ontario Liberals.
I am not much impressed, Mr. Speaker, by the Prime Minister's efforts to propel himself into the role of defender of Canada's unity. The Canadian people are not too willing to forget that it was under his government and because of his political actions that disunity came to Canada. Nor are they too willing to forget that his arrogance and his rigidity as regards constitutional matters are the main reason why so many Quebeckers want out and why the present Quebec government was elected. Recent polls published in Montreal's La Presse also show that opposition to the Prime Minister, his policies and especially his government, has reached an all time high. They are of such nature as to convince voters that maintaining this party in power any longer is the surest way to push a majority of Quebeckers into the arms of the party currently in power in Quebec. Even though the right hon. Prime Minister drapes himself in the Canadian flag in an effort to present the figure of a national hero, he cannot prevent anybody from seeing through the desperate manoeuvre of a politician eager to divert the attention of the public away from the economic chaos in which he has plunged the country and the serious divisions he has created among the various Canadian ethnic groups. Canadians will not fall for this pitch by a man whose credibility has fallen to the zero level. They will remember his stand against controls during the 1974 election campaign. They are not about to forget this huge political fraud, Mr. Speaker.
Should the right hon. Prime Minister decide to masquerade as the saviour of our country, Canadians would only laugh. This so-called rempart against separatism reminds one of the famous rempart the Liberal party claimed it had risen against conscription. It was not very solid. Such ridiculous claims would only make people jeer if they were not accompanied by slanderous remarks against those who oppose the government. Never has there been a party leader, let alone a Prime Minister, who has questioned his adversaries' loyalty to Canada. I do not doubt the sincerity of the leader of the government when he claims that only his policies can save Canada from disaster and I have nothing but pity for his blindness, but I deny him the right to accuse the leader of the opposition or any other public figure for that matter of being disloyal to Canada, just because he happens to favour a greater decentralization of power and a more active role for provincial governments.
Incidently, we have an indication of the sincerity of the right hon. Prime Minister when he states that he is willing to discuss a new power sharing formula with the provinces. The right hon. Prime Minister goes too far when he calls all those who do not agree with him "enemies". This man who claims to be the only one capable of uniting Canadians is the only one who,

November 23, 1978
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
to date, has dared use words likely to provoke division among Canadians and create a truly explosive social climate.
But the worst, Mr. Speaker, is not that the right hon. Prime Minister should have made such unworthy remarks. Today we know that he is quite capable of doing anything at all to save his bacon. The worst is that there should have been Liberals to applaud, to support those unbecoming and unfortunate calls. Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I heard several speeches and I should like to demonstrate the lack of trust in the government that has grown in this country. When the right hon. Prime Minister visited Ontario last Sunday, he went as far as to say that if the country were to have a Progressive Conservative government it would separate. I refuse to accept such a statement, Mr. Speaker. Let us remember the story of the three wisemen.
I feel it is important to recall the time when the right hon. Prime Minister, accompanied by his two attendants, came to Ottawa and decided to sink into the Liberal party. Of course, the Liberals of the day did not see them as their friends and especially not as their counsellors. I would like to remind those who state that the government has managed the affairs of Canada well and who wonder about
(Mr.: Mr. S.]

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to cover all the aspects in this budget we are debating. What I want to do is to expose an outstanding example of a wasteful program, which, if it were cancelled, as it should, could save Canada and its taxpayers $2 billion at least.
Before I deal with that, however, I want to express a few general comments first. I accept the view put forward by my party that this budget does not adequately stimulate the economy or relieve Canada of its depressed economic conditions. To put the matter another way, unemployment will not improve. Indeed, if the prophesies of the U.S. lack of growth are fulfilled, the situation of unemployment in Canada may become a good deal worse. To my way of thinking, unemployment should have the highest priority of all. It should come first in any sound scheme of values in dealing with the economy. I am not thinking only of the economic waste of 1 million employable Canadians making no contribution to the growth and economic prosperity of the country. I am thinking also of the individuals, many of them in my constituency, who are living and will live frustrated lives, not having employment which is the economic base for individual well-being and a necessity to their sense of identity and success in life. I am thinking particularly of those many Canadian children whose lives may well be stunted by the apparent economic failure of their parents.
Why does the minister, who is clearly a man of compassion and intelligence, accept this situation? I can only attribute it to
[Mr.: No, M.J
the devotion of his party to private enterprise. Private enterprise, is not, cannot, and will not do the job or provide the jobs-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -and an industrial strategy in which both private and public enterprise, combined to provide full employment, is essential if we are not to drift on in our present unhappy situation. I have reason to think that the Conservatives would not do any better.

speechtext: That is right.

They equally pay obeisance to private business.
However, to get to the main thrust of what I have to say, we all know that we are in a time of stringency and restraint. Above all, waste in government and private expenditures must be ended. It is tragic that the most conspicuous example of such waste is entirely overlooked by the government. I refer to a matter discussed briefly this afternoon when the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) made a statement concerning the proposed purchase of 130 to 150 fighter planes. Of course, defence and security are high priorities, but they are not sacrosanct. Defence expenditures must be scrutinized like any other expenditures, and firmly resisted if they are not necessary.
The purchase of these planes, we are told, is to cost roughly $2.3 billion in 1977 dollars. With continued inflation and the decline in the Canadian dollar, I would estimate that at least $3 billion is involved. This is by far the greatest expenditure on armaments made in this country in its history. By far the greatest expenditure is to be on manned interceptors to defend this country against a massive bomber attack by the U.S.S.R. Some part of the total no doubt, will be used for providing cover for ground troops in Europe under the provisions of NATO. Whatever may be said now, it is clear that by far the largest amount is to go to the so-called active North American defence.
I propose to show, Mr. Speaker, that these fighter planes are obsolete in the missile age. The essential task of anyone determining the distribution of defence dollars available is to weigh the importance and necessity of the proposed role for our military forces. The task is to weed out those roles not essential to the security of Canada and the stability of the world. There is ample evidence to suggest that fighter planes are not required on a substantial scale in any intelligent consideration of Canada's role. The reason for this is simple, namely, that the threat of a massive Russian attack by manned bombers is non-existent. The allocation of substantial Canadian funds for fighter planes in North America is an outstanding example of the wrong allocation of roles.
I well remember hearing more than ten years ago, in the parliamentary committee on national defence, two very distinguished Canadian soldiers, General Simonds and General Foulkes, who had risen to the top in active service during the

over the world. The need has been suggested in Namibia and in the Middle East; no doubt, other needs will arise. This contributes to the peace of the world, it is something Canada has shown it can do, and it is something we should be prepared to do. We are not against Canada taking a share of responsibility for military commitments, and it is essential that we arm our forces to fulfil these roles. But let us get away from commitment to expenditures that help nobody yet hang a vast debt around the necks of the Canadian people.
All of us are looking at the effects of the cuts that are being made. Many of those cutbacks are painful and unfortunate. We regret the effect they will have on such things as equalization payments, assistance programs, health and medicare. We regret that the cuts affecting the CBC will help destroy the high level of artistic endeavour and quality which has been built up. We object to the CIDA budget being frozen at the expense of those throughout the world who are most in need. We object to the cuts in loans for public housing. We object to the cutting back of forest research stations. There are many acts of this kind, inefficient and selected at random, though some of them are necessary. But let no one say that we in this party did not criticize them and offer alternatives. By all means let us strike out programs and expenditures which we need, to use common parlance, like a hole in the head. The axe must fall, perhaps, but let it fall on what we do not need, on what we could well do without. Let it fall on this unnecessary production of highly sophisticated aircraft whose capability, I believe it is safe to prophesy, will never be used at all. Let us get rid of fantasy and look at the world as it is, making the best contribution we can and minimizing those cutbacks which adversely affect the welfare of the poor, the development of productive resources and the artistic future of this country. Let us use sense about these things and not be swept away by the theory that defence expenditures are sacrosanct. Of course, some are necessary, but none of them are sacrosanct and when we are told by our allies in the United States that the manned bomber is no longer regarded as presenting any considerable risk,-it has been downgraded to almost nothing-why must we go ahead with a project of this kind that we do not need? Is it because we are committed to it, because we do not dare to say no to the military? I believe the military people are wise enough to recognize that it is only when they are doing something worthwhile that they earn the true respect of the people of this country. war, stating that a manned U.S.S.R. bomber over North America would only be possible if the Russians were crazy. They said, that of course, this is not the case.

The important thing is the means of detection. Brian Cuthbertson, writing in "Canadian Military Independence in the Age of the Superpower," published in Toronto in 1977, says, at page 81:
-it appears fairly certain that Soviet strategy sees only a small role for the long-range bomber and for the U.S. anti-bomber defence has become a strategically redundant role.

He goes on to say that the United States plans to reduce its present 405 interceptors to 212 F-106s by the mid-1980s. At page 87, he refers to the strategic redundancy of anti-bomber defence. [DOT]
Mr. James Schlesinger, who was the United States Secretary for Defence, visited Ottawa in September, 1975. That was for the express purpose of consulting about Canada's role in the alliance. He saw the then minister of National Defence, the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson), and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
According to the report which I have, dated September 27, 1975, he played down the Soviet bomb threat and urged Canada instead to beef up its forces and equipment in Europe. To use his own words, well equipped ground forces in Europe would be the most illustrious contribution Canada could make to western security.
In 1977, Mr. Cuthbertson wrote about the weaknesses of NORAD in the following words. He referred to the vulnerability of its installation to destruction by missiles, its poor capability in the detection of low level flights and lack of capability against bombers launching missiles outside the interceptor range.
These circumstances demonstrate that the defence of North America depends upon maintenance by the United States of a retaliatory force, either in fixed sites, ICBMs, which may become vulnerable-they have not yet, but they may-or in submarines equipped with missiles which are not now, and are
The Budget-Mr. Brewin
not likely in the foreseeable future, to become vulnerable. This submarine-based force exists and is not likely to be substantially reduced by technical changes for many years to come.
It is suggested by some that the Russian development of the backfire bomber has changed all this. The Russians presently have 50 backfire bombers in commission, according to the International Institute of Strategic Studies Military Balance for 1978-79. That is not a great many.
They lack intercontinental range, but with a compatible tanker force can be refueled in flight. It would not be correct or fair to say they could not reach North America directly. They are also capable of flying below radar detection. Cuthbertson suggests that when employed with a tanker force, they would have a "peripheral role". However that may be, there are two main defences: the first is the same as the defence against any manned bomber, namely the impossibility of destroying an effective retaliatory force and therefore the assurance that the use of such bombers would provoke a retaliation which would destroy the U.S.S.R. as a functioning society. The second is that efforts could be made to improve the detection capacity of defence forces in North America.
It is sometimes said that Canada's commitments under NORAD, while strategically useless, are justifiable on political grounds. When this question of the political grounds is pressed, it appears that the political ground is the view that the United States desires the continuing of NORAD and of the Canadian contribution to a fighter anti-bomber.
There is no evidence to support this. Indeed, the view expressed by Mr. Schlesinger is exactly the opposite of this, as is the down-grading of the American interceptors to a secondary role.
When pressed for positive evidence, neither the former minister of National Defence nor the present President of Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), who was then Secretary of State for External Affairs, could give any basis whatever for their statement that the United States was anxious that the NORAD arrangement be continued. Indeed, the former minister of National Defence in the committee or. external affairs, said that his belief was based on a conversation with an unnamed person at NATO and was not supported by any documents or evidence whatsoever. The same is true of the similar claim asserted by the then Secretary of State for External Affairs, now President of Privy Council. It would indeed be a strange surrender of Canadian judgment if we were to be governed in our views of policy by a non-existent, non-proven political view that the United States desired Canada to maintain this role, in view of their own actions and their own words and the clear indication that an anti-bomber is strategically redundant in their eyes.
